questions.stem: An 84 year old woman is brought in by her carer during a heatwave. She has been drinking very little for 4 days and is drowsy. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 102/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Her mouth is dry. Urine dipstick is negative for leucocytes and nitrites.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Reduced intake has caused a body water deficit, with the classic raised urea:creatinine ratio, hypernatraemia and high haematocrit. Normal glucose excludes HHS.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Poor intake in **hot weather**, tachycardia, dry mouth, and bloods with **high urea out of proportion to creatinine**, high sodium and high haematocrit.

elim: Her saturations are normal and she has signs of volume depletion, not overload.
Her glucose is normal.
Causes hyponatraemia; her sodium is high.
The dipstick is negative for leucocytes and nitrites and she has no fever.

steps.x: **B. Dehydration.** Raised urea:creatinine ratio, hypernatraemia and a high haematocrit is the classic dehydration picture.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has had diarrhoea 8 times a day for 3 days after a family meal. He feels weak and lightheaded. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 108/66 mmHg and respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute. His abdomen is soft and non-tender.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
questions.e: Fluid loss from diarrhoea causes dehydration with reduced skin turgor, sunken eyes and tachycardia. Raised JVP, crackles and oedema are signs of fluid overload.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on examination? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: diarrhoea 8 times a day for 3 days
steps.x: Fluid loss from **diarrhoea** with **tachycardia**: he is volume deplete.

elim: A sign of pulmonary oedema from fluid overload.
Seen with a high-output state or aortic regurgitation, not volume depletion.
Suggests fluid overload or low albumin.
Suggests fluid overload; the JVP is low in dehydration.

steps.x: **E. Reduced skin turgor.** Dehydration signs: dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, sunken eyes, tachycardia, oliguria.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman has had vomiting and diarrhoea for 5 days. She is now confused and drowsy. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 78/46 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Her peripheries are cold, capillary refill time is 5 seconds and she has not passed urine for 12 hours.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate assessment of her condition?
o: Pre-renal acute kidney injury without dehydration
questions.e: Hypotension, confusion and tachycardia mark severe dehydration, where circulating volume has fallen below the level needed to perfuse organs (hypovolaemic shock). Mild dehydration causes only thirst and dry mouth.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most accurate assessment of her condition? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Hypotension, confusion, tachycardia** and no urine after fluid losses.

elim: Mild dehydration causes thirst and a dry mouth with normal observations.
She is hypotensive, confused and anuric, which are features of shock.
Pre-renal AKI here would be a result of the dehydration, not an alternative to it.
She has no fever and a clear cause of volume loss, with cold peripheries.

steps.x: **E. Severe dehydration with hypovolaemic shock.** Severe dehydration = hypotension, confusion, shock and tachycardia: give IV 0.9% saline.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has had food poisoning for 24 hours with 4 episodes of vomiting, which have now stopped. She feels thirsty and has a dry mouth. She is alert and drinking. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 122/78 mmHg and respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute. She has passed urine twice today.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate assessment of her hydration?
questions.e: Thirst and dry mouth with normal observations is mild-to-moderate dehydration, treated with oral rehydration solution. Severe dehydration causes hypotension, confusion and tachycardia.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most accurate assessment of her hydration? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: thirsty and has a dry mouth
steps.x: **Thirst and dry mouth** with **normal observations** and normal mental state.

elim: Her pulse and BP are normal.
She is thirsty with a dry mouth after fluid losses.
She is passing urine and has no evidence of reduced kidney function.
There is no hypotension, confusion or tachycardia.

steps.x: **B. Mild-to-moderate dehydration.** Assess severity first: mild-moderate (thirst, dry mouth) gets ORS; severe gets IV fluids.

questions.stem: An 81 year old man is admitted after a week of poor oral intake. His pulse rate is 100 bpm and BP 110/68 mmHg. Investigations: sodium 146 mmol/L (135–145), potassium 4.6 mmol/L (3.5–5.3), urea 21.0 mmol/L (2.5–7.8), creatinine 118 µmol/L (60–110), albumin 38 g/L (35–50). His baseline creatinine is 100 µmol/L.
questions.q: Which feature of these results most strongly supports dehydration?
o: Disproportionate rise in urea relative to creatinine
Small rise in creatinine above baseline
Sodium at the upper limit of normal
questions.e: A disproportionate rise in urea relative to creatinine is the classic marker of dehydration, because urea is reabsorbed with water while creatinine is not. A small creatinine rise alone is non-specific.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which feature of these results most strongly supports dehydration? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Urea has nearly **tripled** while creatinine has barely moved.

elim: A normal albumin does not point towards or away from dehydration.
Potassium can be normal, high or low in dehydration.
Creatinine rises only a little; on its own it does not separate dehydration from other causes.
Supportive but less specific than the urea:creatinine ratio.

steps.x: **A. Disproportionate rise in urea relative to creatinine.** A raised urea:creatinine ratio is the signature of a pre-renal, volume-depleted state.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man has had profuse watery diarrhoea for 6 days and has struggled to drink. He has passed 200 mL of urine in 24 hours. His pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 94/58 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows no blood or protein. A bladder scan shows 40 mL. His creatinine was 82 µmol/L last month.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his kidney injury?
questions.e: Dehydration reduces renal perfusion and causes pre-renal acute kidney injury, with a disproportionate rise in urea. A clear dipstick and empty bladder make glomerulonephritis and obstruction unlikely.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his kidney injury? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Fluid loss, **low urine output**, bland urine and no obstruction: the kidneys are under-perfused.

elim: Usually drug-induced with rash, eosinophilia or white cells in the urine.
Causes blood and protein on the dipstick.
The bladder scan shows only 40 mL.
No muscle injury is described, and the dipstick shows no blood.

steps.x: **D. Pre-renal acute kidney injury.** Dehydration's key complication is pre-renal AKI; the urea rises out of proportion to creatinine.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man had a stroke 6 days ago and has an unsafe swallow. He is nil by mouth and his intravenous cannula has fallen out twice. He is drowsier than yesterday. His pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. His tongue is dry. Glucose is 6.4 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his dehydration?
questions.e: He has been nil by mouth with interrupted IV access, so reduced fluid intake is the cause. A normal glucose excludes osmotic diuresis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his dehydration? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
He has had **no oral or IV fluid** for days.

elim: No steroid history, and hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia would be expected.
Would cause polyuria with dilute urine; a stroke rarely causes it.
His glucose is normal.
Causes hyponatraemia with water retention, not dehydration.

steps.x: **D. Reduced fluid intake.** Causes: vomiting, diarrhoea, reduced intake and osmotic diuresis in diabetes.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman has had vomiting and diarrhoea for 2 days after a holiday. She feels dizzy when she stands up and is very thirsty. Her temperature is 37.5°C and respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute. Her mucous membranes are dry and her eyes look sunken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on her observations?
questions.e: Reduced circulating volume causes a compensatory tachycardia, alongside dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes and dizziness. Bradycardia and hypertension are not features.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on her observations? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Fluid loss with **dizziness**, dry mucous membranes and **sunken eyes**.

elim: Volume loss triggers a reflex rise in heart rate, not a fall.
Volume depletion lowers, not raises, BP.
Dehydration does not affect gas exchange.
The pulse pressure narrows as stroke volume falls.

steps.x: **D. Tachycardia.** Reduced circulating volume gives a compensatory tachycardia.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man is referred by his GP because of a high haemoglobin found during a week of diarrhoea and poor intake. He has never smoked and has no lung disease. His pulse rate is 102 bpm and BP 108/64 mmHg. He has no splenomegaly. A previous full blood count 3 months ago was normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the blood count?
questions.e: Loss of body water concentrates the blood, raising the haemoglobin and haematocrit (relative polycythaemia), along with a raised urea. Polycythaemia vera is a true increase in red cell mass with splenomegaly.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely explanation for the blood count? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: week of diarrhoea and poor intake
steps.x: A **new** high haemoglobin and haematocrit with **raised urea** during fluid loss.

elim: Would not appear within 3 months alongside acute fluid loss, and would not explain the raised urea.
Usually causes splenomegaly and raised white cells and platelets, and his count was normal 3 months ago.
He has no lung disease or smoking history.
He has never smoked.

steps.x: **A. Dehydration.** Haemoconcentration: loss of plasma water gives a high haematocrit (relative polycythaemia).

questions.stem: An 89 year old woman with advanced dementia has been eating and drinking very little for a week. She is drowsy. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 104/62 mmHg. Her urine is dark and scanty. Investigations: sodium 155 mmol/L (135–145), urea 17.5 mmol/L (2.5–7.8), creatinine 98 µmol/L (45–90), glucose 6.0 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her hypernatraemia?
questions.e: A net loss of water relative to sodium concentrates the plasma, giving hypernatraemia with concentrated urine. Diabetes insipidus causes dilute urine.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her hypernatraemia? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: eating and drinking very little for a week
steps.x: Poor intake, **concentrated urine**, high urea: she has lost more water than sodium.

elim: Causes mild hypernatraemia with hypertension and hypokalaemia, not volume depletion.
Produces large volumes of dilute urine; hers is dark and scanty.
She has not received intravenous fluid.
Her glucose is normal.

steps.x: **E. Water deficit from dehydration.** Hypernatraemia in dehydration reflects a net water deficit.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has had severe vomiting for 4 days and cannot keep fluids down. He is confused. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 132 bpm, BP 80/50 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. His peripheries are cold and clammy, his JVP is not visible and his chest is clear. ECG shows sinus tachycardia only.
questions.q: Which is the most likely type of shock?
questions.e: Severe dehydration from vomiting has reduced circulating volume below the level needed for organ perfusion, causing hypovolaemic shock. A non-visible JVP and clear chest argue against cardiogenic shock.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely type of shock? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Large **fluid losses**, cold peripheries and an **empty JVP**.

elim: No allergen exposure, urticaria, wheeze or angioedema.
The JVP is not visible, the chest is clear and the ECG shows only sinus tachycardia.
Follows spinal cord injury and causes bradycardia with warm peripheries.
He has no fever or source of infection, and his peripheries are cold.

steps.x: **C. Hypovolaemic shock.** Severe dehydration causes hypovolaemic shock when circulating volume falls too low to perfuse organs.

questions.stem: An 82 year old woman is admitted with 3 days of fatigue and dizziness. She has had a cold and has not felt like drinking. She takes no regular medicines. Her pulse rate is 100 bpm and BP 112/66 mmHg. Her mucous membranes are dry. She has no melaena and her rectal examination is normal. Urine dipstick is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Poor intake with dry mucous membranes and a disproportionately raised urea is dehydration. An upper GI bleed also raises urea but she has no melaena and her haemoglobin is high.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Poor intake, dry mucous membranes and a **high urea:creatinine ratio** with no bleeding.

elim: The creatinine is only mildly raised and the urea is raised far out of proportion.
Her glucose is normal.
Can also raise urea, but she has no melaena and her haemoglobin is high.
The urine dipstick is negative.

steps.x: **B. Dehydration.** Raised urea out of proportion to creatinine = dehydration (or upper GI bleed, so check for melaena).

questions.stem: A 75 year old man is admitted with dehydration after a week of diarrhoea. He is not catheterised. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 106/64 mmHg. The nurse is asked to start a fluid balance chart and record his urine output for the next 12 hours before fluids take effect.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his fluid balance chart?
o: Frequent small volumes of pale urine
questions.e: In dehydration the kidneys conserve water, producing oliguria with concentrated, dark urine. Large volumes of pale urine suggest diabetes insipidus.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on his fluid balance chart? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: dehydration after a week of diarrhoea
steps.x: Volume depletion makes the kidneys **save water**.

elim: Suggests urinary retention, not dehydration.
Pale urine is dilute; dehydration produces concentrated urine.
Volume falls in dehydration.
Polyuria with dilute urine suggests diabetes insipidus or diuretic use.

steps.x: **E. Small volumes of dark urine.** Dehydration causes oliguria with concentrated, low-volume urine.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman is admitted with 3 days of vomiting. She is thirsty and dizzy, with a dry tongue, reduced skin turgor and a pulse rate of 102 bpm. Her BP is 110/70 mmHg. The medical student asks which single assessment best confirms that she is dehydrated.
questions.q: Which is the gold standard for diagnosing dehydration?
questions.e: Clinical assessment of history and examination is the gold standard for dehydration. Blood and urine tests support it and look for complications.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the gold standard for diagnosing dehydration? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
The history and examination already show **thirst, dry tongue, poor turgor and tachycardia**.

elim: Does not assess hydration.
Assesses cardiac function, not the diagnosis of dehydration.
Not a measure of body water deficit.
Can support a pre-renal state but does not confirm dehydration on its own.

steps.x: **B. Clinical assessment.** Dehydration is a clinical diagnosis; bloods support it and assess severity.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man is admitted after 5 days of diarrhoea and poor intake. He is dizzy on standing. His pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 104/62 mmHg. His blood results are sent.
questions.q: Which pattern on urea and electrolytes is most likely?
o: Low urea, low sodium and normal creatinine
Normal urea, low sodium and high potassium
Normal urea, normal sodium and raised creatinine
Raised urea, low sodium and low creatinine
Raised urea, raised sodium and raised creatinine
questions.e: U&Es in dehydration show raised urea (the most sensitive marker), raised sodium and raised creatinine. Low sodium with low urea suggests water excess such as SIADH.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which pattern on urea and electrolytes is most likely? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: 5 days of diarrhoea and poor intake
steps.x: Water loss concentrates the blood and reduces renal perfusion.

elim: Typical of SIADH or water overload.
Suggests adrenal insufficiency.
Suggests chronic kidney disease or a high muscle mass, not dehydration.
Creatinine rises, not falls, with volume depletion.

steps.x: **E. Raised urea, raised sodium and raised creatinine.** U&Es first-line: raised urea (most sensitive), raised sodium, raised creatinine.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman has had poor intake for a week. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Her urea is 15.2 mmol/L and creatinine 101 µmol/L. The team wants a second-line test to show that her kidneys are appropriately conserving water.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: In dehydration, ADH makes the kidneys produce concentrated urine with a high osmolality. Ultrasound and protein tests do not measure water conservation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
The question asks for a test of **urine concentration**.

elim: Looks for obstruction or kidney size, not water conservation.
Not a test of renal water handling.
Looks for infection.
Quantifies proteinuria, not urine concentration.

steps.x: **D. Urine osmolality.** Second-line: urine tests show concentrated urine with high osmolality.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man has had 2 weeks of extreme thirst, passing large volumes of urine and losing 5 kg in weight. He is now dizzy. His pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. His mucous membranes are dry. He has no vomiting or diarrhoea.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional investigation to find the cause of his dehydration?
questions.e: Polyuria, thirst and weight loss suggest dehydration from diabetic osmotic diuresis, so blood glucose is checked. A water deprivation test is dangerous when he is already dehydrated.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate additional investigation to find the cause of his dehydration? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Thirst, **polyuria** and weight loss: dehydration from **osmotic diuresis**.

elim: Hypercalcaemia can cause polyuria, but weight loss in a young man points first to diabetes.
He has no diarrhoea.
Hyperthyroidism causes weight loss but not marked polyuria.
Not done in a dehydrated patient, and diabetes must be excluded first.

steps.x: **A. Blood glucose.** Additional tests in dehydration: blood glucose and FBC.

questions.stem: A 65 year old woman is admitted with dehydration after 4 days of vomiting. Her U&Es show a raised urea and sodium. The registrar asks for one more routine blood test that would show haemoconcentration.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: A full blood count shows a raised haematocrit in dehydration because plasma water is lost. CRP and coagulation tests do not reflect plasma volume.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Haemoconcentration shows as a **high haematocrit**, which is on the blood count.

elim: An inflammatory marker, not a measure of haemoconcentration.
Does not reflect plasma volume.
Do not show haemoconcentration.
Useful in vomiting but does not show haemoconcentration.

steps.x: **C. Full blood count.** Additional tests: blood glucose and FBC (high haematocrit).

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with severe dehydration is given intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride. His results over the first 48 hours are shown (see item resources). He is improving clinically and the team is deciding how to monitor his fluid treatment.

visual.title: Serum sodium during IV fluids
visual.caption: Sodium falls gradually, by less than 10 mmol/L per 24 hours, as he is rehydrated.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to monitor treatment?
questions.e: U&Es track urea, sodium and potassium during rehydration so electrolytes can be corrected carefully and slowly. A blood count alone does not show sodium or potassium.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation to monitor treatment? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Rehydration must be tracked with **sodium, potassium and urea**.

elim: Only needed if fluid overload is suspected.
Not used to monitor routine rehydration.
Monitors inflammation, not fluid or electrolyte balance.
Does not show sodium or potassium.

steps.x: **E. Repeat urea and electrolytes.** Correct electrolytes carefully, monitoring sodium and potassium; correct slowly.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man sees his GP after 2 days of diarrhoea. He feels thirsty and has a dry mouth. He is alert and drinking. His pulse rate is 86 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg and temperature 37.3°C. He is passing urine normally.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: He has mild-to-moderate dehydration, so oral rehydration solution is first-line. IV fluids are for severe dehydration with hypotension or confusion.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: thirsty and has a dry mouth
steps.x: First **assess severity**: thirst and dry mouth with normal observations is mild-to-moderate.

elim: IV fluids are for severe dehydration; he is alert with normal observations.
Reserved for severe burns when crystalloid is not enough.
Does not replace the fluid he has lost.
Antibiotics are not routine for mild diarrhoea and do not rehydrate him.

steps.x: **E. Oral rehydration solution.** Mild-to-moderate dehydration: oral rehydration solution first-line.

questions.stem: An 87 year old woman is admitted from a nursing home after 4 days of diarrhoea. She is confused. Her pulse rate is 122 bpm, BP 84/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and capillary refill time 4 seconds. Her chest is clear and there is no ankle oedema. Glucose is 6.1 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate fluid for initial resuscitation?
questions.e: Severe dehydration with hypotension and confusion needs IV 0.9% sodium chloride. Glucose solutions spread into all body water and do not restore circulating volume.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate fluid for initial resuscitation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Hypotension and confusion: **severe dehydration** needing IV resuscitation.

elim: Hypotonic fluid is not used for resuscitation.
Used for hypoglycaemia, not volume replacement.
Distributes into all body water and does not stay in the circulation.
Reserved for severe burns when crystalloid alone is not enough.

steps.x: **B. 0.9% sodium chloride.** Severe dehydration: IV 0.9% saline.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has severe dehydration from vomiting. His pulse rate is 124 bpm, BP 86/54 mmHg and he is drowsy. He has no history of heart failure. Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride is prescribed, following NICE guidance on intravenous fluid therapy in adults in hospital (NG29).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial fluid bolus?
questions.e: NICE NG29 recommends a 500 mL bolus of crystalloid such as 0.9% sodium chloride over less than 15 minutes, then reassessment. The slower options are maintenance rates.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial fluid bolus? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A shocked patient needs **resuscitation**, not maintenance fluid.

elim: A maintenance rate, far too slow for resuscitation.
Too large a single bolus without reassessment.
Too slow for a shocked patient.
A maintenance-style rate, not resuscitation.

steps.x: **E. 500 mL over less than 15 minutes.** NICE NG29: 500 mL crystalloid bolus over less than 15 minutes, then reassess.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with severe dehydration from gastroenteritis has received a 500 mL bolus of intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride. On reassessment her pulse rate is 114 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg and capillary refill time 4 seconds. Her chest is clear and she has no oedema.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Further 500 mL bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride and reassess
Switch to 5% glucose at maintenance rate
questions.e: She remains severely dehydrated without overload, so she needs a further 500 mL bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride and reassessment. Oral fluids are only for mild-to-moderate dehydration.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Still **tachycardic and hypotensive** with no signs of overload.

elim: She is still volume deplete; a diuretic would worsen it.
She is still shocked; oral fluid is for mild-to-moderate dehydration.
Vasopressors are not the next step when she has only had one bolus and is fluid responsive.
Maintenance glucose does not restore circulating volume.

steps.x: **A. Further 500 mL bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride and reassess.** Reassess after each bolus; repeat if still volume deplete.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has had 4 days of vomiting and is moderately dehydrated. He cannot tolerate oral fluids. His pulse rate is 100 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Investigations: sodium 141 mmol/L (135–145), potassium 2.9 mmol/L (3.5–5.3), urea 12.0 mmol/L (2.5–7.8). He is to be given intravenous fluids.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate intravenous fluid?
questions.e: He needs volume and potassium replacement, so 0.9% sodium chloride with added potassium chloride is given with U&E monitoring. Bicarbonate would worsen the alkalosis of vomiting.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate intravenous fluid? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Fluid deficit plus **low potassium** from vomiting.

elim: Bicarbonate would worsen the metabolic alkalosis of vomiting.
Does not replace sodium or potassium.
Does not replace sodium or potassium and does not stay in the circulation.
Reserved for burns; it does not correct potassium.

steps.x: **A. 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium chloride.** Correct electrolytes carefully during rehydration, monitoring sodium and potassium.

questions.stem: An 85 year old woman is admitted after a week of poor intake. She is drowsy. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg. Her sodium is 162 mmol/L (135–145) and urea 19.0 mmol/L (2.5–7.8). Fluids are started and the team plans how quickly to bring her sodium down.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate target rate of sodium correction?
o: As fast as possible to normal
No more than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours
Wait until sodium normalises without fluids
questions.e: Hypernatraemic dehydration must be corrected slowly, by no more than about 10 mmol/L in 24 hours, because adapted brain cells take up water and swell if sodium falls quickly.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate target rate of sodium correction? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: how quickly to bring her sodium down
steps.x: Chronic **hypernatraemic dehydration**: brain cells have adapted, so go slowly.

elim: Rapid correction risks cerebral oedema.
Too fast; brain cells adapted to hypertonicity swell.
Far too fast and risks cerebral oedema and seizures.
She is dehydrated and needs fluid.

steps.x: **C. No more than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours.** Correct sodium slowly (no more than about 10 mmol/L per 24 hours) to avoid cerebral oedema.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman with type 2 diabetes was admitted with dehydration from osmotic diuresis. Her glucose was 24 mmol/L. After 24 hours of intravenous fluids she is drinking, her urea has normalised and her BP is 128/78 mmHg. She takes metformin only and her HbA1c is 98 mmol/mol.
questions.q: Which is the most important step before discharge to prevent recurrence?
o: Continue intravenous fluids for a further 48 hours
Fluid restriction to 1.5 litres a day
questions.e: Her dehydration was caused by osmotic diuresis from poorly controlled diabetes, so treating the underlying cause by optimising glycaemic control prevents recurrence.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most important step before discharge to prevent recurrence? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
The cause of her dehydration is **uncontrolled diabetes**.

elim: She is now drinking and her urea has normalised.
Does not address the cause.
Would worsen dehydration.
Would increase fluid losses.

steps.x: **D. Optimise her glycaemic control.** Treat the underlying cause: infection, diabetes, vomiting or diarrhoea.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has 35% total body surface area partial-thickness burns from a kitchen fire. She has received crystalloid by the burns formula for 18 hours. She remains hypotensive with a urine output of 0.2 mL/kg/hour and increasing tissue oedema. Her albumin is 18 g/L.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate fluid?
o: Further crystalloid only at double the rate
questions.e: In severe burns where crystalloid resuscitation alone is insufficient, human albumin solution helps restore intravascular volume and limits oedema. More crystalloid would worsen oedema.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate fluid? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: crystalloid by the burns formula for 18 hours
steps.x: Major burns where **crystalloid alone is not enough** and oedema is worsening.

elim: Hypotonic fluid will worsen oedema and not stay in the circulation.
Distributes into all body water and does not restore circulating volume.
Crystalloid has failed and more will increase oedema.
Not adequate for a hypotensive patient with major burns.

steps.x: **D. Human albumin solution.** Severe burns with insufficient crystalloid response: Human Albumin Solution (HAS).

questions.stem: A 90 year old man is admitted after lying on the floor for 2 days in a warm room without water. He has lost more water than sodium. His sodium is 157 mmol/L (135–145) and serum osmolality 330 mOsm/kg (275–295). His pulse rate is 102 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg.
questions.q: Which type of dehydration does he have?
questions.e: Losing more water than sodium raises sodium and osmolality: hypertonic dehydration. Equal loss is isotonic and greater sodium loss is hypotonic.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which type of dehydration does he have? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**High sodium and osmolality**: water loss exceeds sodium loss.

elim: Sodium loss exceeds water loss, giving a low sodium.
Equal loss of water and sodium keeps sodium normal.
A laboratory artefact of low sodium with lipids or protein.
Excess water with low sodium.

steps.x: **A. Hypertonic dehydration.** Dehydration can be isotonic, hypotonic or hypertonic depending on relative water and electrolyte loss.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man has had profuse diarrhoea for 5 days and has replaced his losses by drinking large amounts of plain tap water. He is dizzy and tachycardic with a dry mouth. His sodium is 127 mmol/L (135–145) and urea 11.8 mmol/L (2.5–7.8).
questions.q: Which type of dehydration does he most likely have?
questions.e: Losing sodium in diarrhoea and replacing it with plain water leaves him volume deplete with a low sodium: hypotonic dehydration. SIADH causes hyponatraemia without volume depletion.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which type of dehydration does he most likely have? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Salt lost in diarrhoea, **replaced with water only**, so sodium falls while he stays volume deplete.

elim: This needs water loss in excess of sodium, giving a high sodium.
His sodium is low, not normal.
Causes water excess, not a volume deficit with a raised urea.
Causes euvolaemic hyponatraemia, not tachycardia and a raised urea.

steps.x: **B. Hypotonic dehydration.** Relative loss of electrolytes over water gives hypotonic dehydration.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman is dehydrated after a week of poor intake. Her urine osmolality is 860 mOsm/kg (300–900). A medical student asks which hormone is mainly responsible for the insertion of aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting duct, allowing her to produce such concentrated urine.
questions.q: Which hormone is responsible?
questions.e: Reduced circulating volume triggers ADH release, which inserts aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting duct so water is reabsorbed and urine is concentrated. Aldosterone, via RAAS, increases sodium reabsorption.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which hormone is responsible? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Concentrated urine depends on **water reabsorption** in the collecting duct.

elim: Increases sodium reabsorption in the distal nephron but does not insert aquaporin-2.
Released with volume overload and promotes sodium and water loss.
Not the main regulator of collecting duct water permeability.
Regulates calcium and phosphate.

steps.x: **B. Antidiuretic hormone.** Low volume activates RAAS and ADH release, increasing water and sodium reabsorption.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man is dehydrated after 4 days of diarrhoea. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg. His urine sodium is 8 mmol/L, showing that his kidneys are retaining sodium avidly. He takes no diuretics.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his low urine sodium?
questions.e: Reduced circulating volume activates the RAAS; aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption so urine sodium is low. In acute tubular necrosis the tubules cannot hold on to sodium.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of his low urine sodium? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Low renal perfusion switches on **renin, angiotensin and aldosterone**.

elim: Damaged tubules cannot retain sodium, so urine sodium is high.
ANP rises with volume overload and increases sodium excretion.
ADH rises, not falls, in dehydration.
Renin rises when renal perfusion falls.

steps.x: **A. Activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.** RAAS activation increases renal sodium (and water) reabsorption.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman with dehydration has a urea of 24.0 mmol/L (2.5–7.8) but a creatinine of only 112 µmol/L (45–90). The foundation doctor asks why creatinine has risen so much less than urea.
questions.q: Which property of creatinine best explains this?
o: It is actively reabsorbed in the loop of Henle
It is broken down by the liver when perfusion falls
It is not reabsorbed with water in the tubule
It is produced only during exercise
It is secreted into the bile
questions.e: Urea is passively reabsorbed with water in the proximal tubule, so it rises disproportionately when water is conserved. Creatinine is not reabsorbed, so it rises much less.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which property of creatinine best explains this? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: risen so much less than urea
steps.x: Urea follows water back into the blood; **creatinine does not**.

elim: Creatinine is not reabsorbed; this would raise it, not lower it.
Creatinine is not hepatically cleared in this way.
Creatinine is produced continuously from muscle creatine.
It is cleared by the kidneys, not the bile.

steps.x: **C. It is not reabsorbed with water in the tubule.** Urea is reabsorbed passively with water in the proximal tubule; creatinine is unaffected.
